Holidays and family

Christmas with an alcoholic family member: how to get through the holidays

Not a plan for a perfect Christmas. A plan for making it through with more steadiness and safety.

Steven H. White · approximately 9 min read

“You cannot decide what they will do. You can decide what you will accept—and when you will leave.”

This article shares personal experience and general information. It is not a substitute for medical, psychological, or addiction care.

Most of us carry a picture of Christmas: light, warmth, the family together, laughter around the table. Then there is another picture we speak about less often—the tense wait to see what they will be like today. The question of which drink will change their voice. The moment when you may need to invent an explanation for the relatives.

If you know that second picture, this article is for you. Not to tell you how to create a perfect holiday, but to make it a little easier to get through.

Why can the holidays feel harder?

During the rest of the year, drinking often has outside limits: work, early mornings, ordinary routines. Over the holidays, those limits loosen. People are off work, guests come and go, and alcohol appears almost everywhere. Champagne, mulled wine, a toast with relatives. For someone who is dependent on alcohol, the season can become less of a challenge than a disguise.

My Christmases

In my family, it was normal for everyone to drink during celebrations. As a child, that seemed natural. Later, when I drank too, I did not look forward to the food. I looked forward to being able to drink all day.

As time passed, my drinking began to cause harm in what I said and what I did. Pressure came from every direction. The holidays became “legitimate” drinking: at Christmas people challenged me less, there was less conflict, I could let go, and everyone treated it as normal. That was why I waited for it so eagerly.

In my twenties, two friends, the woman I loved, and I decided to go to midnight Mass. We did go. Beforehand, while we talked, we finished two bottles of spirits between us. To us, that was normal.

Later, when I was married, Christmas meant presents, drinking, and television if we stayed home. Most years, the full day of preparation—much of it spent moving the tree from one place to another—had already produced the “right” amount to drink.

I do not know when my family first noticed. Probably when I was a teenager, though it was easy to explain away then: it is a holiday; he is young. I will never know exactly when it became a problem. It did not look like one to me. Looking back now, I can see that it was a problem for the people around me. I always had an explanation.

For me, “Christmas and love” had become a dishonest performance. Alcohol had been driving the day for a long time.

The holidays also bring expectations: make it beautiful, make it happy, do not spoil it. The person living beside the drinker carries even more—the food, gifts, guests, and the extra task of making sure nobody notices what is really happening.

Before: two or three weeks ahead

Decide what you want. Not what you want them to do—you cannot decide that. Ask what matters to you. A calm evening with the children? Not having to carry everything alone? One day when you are not constantly watching? When you know what you want, it is easier to protect it.

Let go of the perfect holiday. The larger the expectation, the deeper the disappointment can be. A simpler Christmas with fewer plans and fewer guests is often easier to live through. You do not have to repeat last year or copy anyone else.

Make your own plan.

1. Your own transportation. If you are visiting relatives, make sure you can leave when you choose. Do not let their condition determine who drives.

2. One ally. Choose a sibling, friend, or relative who knows what is happening and whom you can message when things become difficult.

3. A plan for the children. Know where they can go if the atmosphere changes and who can stay with them if you need to leave.

4. One sentence you can say. For example: “I am taking the children home now.” A sentence prepared in advance is much easier to use.

During the holiday

Do not argue with someone who is intoxicated. This is one of the most important points. Alcohol impairs judgment, and an argument started in that moment usually ends worse than it began. If something needs to be discussed, it can wait for a sober time.

You do not have to put on a show. Many people spend the holiday hiding what is happening from relatives. They make excuses, explain it away, and take over the drinker’s responsibilities. You do not need to tell everyone everything, but you do not have to conceal it at any cost. If someone asks, it can be enough to say, “Yes, we are going through a difficult time.”

Take breaks. Walk the dog, call someone, spend ten minutes alone in the bathroom. That is not running away; it is taking a breath. Nobody can remain intensely watchful all day without a pause.

If your family member is sober or trying to stop

The holiday can still be difficult when the person is not drinking. Alcohol is everywhere and people keep offering it. It can help to have good alcohol-free choices on the table and not turn their sobriety into the family’s main topic. But their sobriety remains their responsibility. You do not have to guard the bottles.

After: the days that follow

Many people wake after the holidays exhausted and disappointed. That is understandable. Do not decide the future of your whole relationship on December 27, when you are at your most depleted. But do not erase what you saw and felt either. Write it down. A month later, with a clearer mind, it may matter.

In January, many people try an alcohol-free month or Dry January. If your partner plans to do this, it may be a useful beginning. Notice how difficult it is for them and what the month reveals. But do not make your own peace depend on whether they succeed.

A few questions for yourself

What do I want from this holiday, regardless of what they do?

What did I do last year that I do not want to do again?

Who can I contact if things become difficult?

How will I get home if I decide to leave?

If you are afraid

If drinking turns into aggression, if you are afraid, or if you or your children may be in danger, do not stay. Go somewhere safe and call emergency services if there is immediate danger.

Steven H. White has been sober for ten years. Today, he celebrates sober.

The goal is not a perfect Christmas

What matters is having your own plan, your own way home, and at least one person who knows what is happening. Safety matters more than appearances.

One calmer next step

You do not have to solve everything in a single day.

It is enough to know what matters to you, whom you can call, and when you will leave. A holiday does not overrule your safety.
